newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong investors bank on Shanghai economic boom.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong investors bank on Shanghai economic boom.

text.p: Hong Kong investors will continue to pour billions of U.S. dollars into Shanghai to take advantage of Chinese government backing for the city and to avoid risk at home, analysts and business officials said.

The British colony of Hong Kong -- which reverts to Chinese rule on June 30 -- is already by far the largest foreign investor in Shanghai with accumulated investment of $20.85 billion at the end of 1996, according to official figures.

"Shanghai has the support of the central government and will be the 'dragon head' to lead the economic development of the whole Yangtze River region," said Wing Sham, director of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council's Shanghai office.

Investment in Shanghai allows Hong Kong firms to diversify given the lower economic growth rates now in their home city and the risk of depending on an income base that is too narrow, according to analysts.

"Although Hong Kong can expect steady growth, we'll never see growth of seven to eight percent in the coming years," said Hang Seng Bank economist Joanne Yim. "That's why companies have changed their focus and invested in China."
Yim predicts Hong Kong's economy will grow 5.4 percent in 1997, compared with Shanghai's official forecast of 10 percent.

The Hong Kong money flooding into Shanghai is in a way a pay-back for help in the past -- Shanghai industrialists who fled China in 1949, when the Chinese Communist Party took power, helped build Hong Kong into an economic powerhouse.

In the 1980s, Hong Kong moved the bulk of its manufacturing industry across the border to Guangdong province which offered cheap prices and abundant labour and the convenience of a common Chinese dialect.

Shanghai, which like Hong Kong more than a decade ago is currently shifting away from labour-intensive industries, now offers Hong Kong companies more sophisticated investment opportunities than Guangdong.
"It's just a way to diversify," said Hang Seng Bank's Yim. "Companies in Hong Kong have grown to such size they want to diversify their profit base."
Shanghai's advantages encouraged Hong Kong to invest $3.86 billion in the city in 1996 and $3.65 billion in 1995, largely in the property and service sectors.

For Hong Kong's Lai Sun Development, Shanghai's 15 percent guaranteed return for investment in residential housing for locals and its plan to spend roughly 333 billion yuan on infrastructure from 1996 to 2000 is too much to resist.
"The reason why we invest in Shanghai is because it is one of the major cities that seems more promising," said a Lai Sun official.
For the colony's Hang Seng Bank, the lure of Shanghai is the city's promise to open its banking sector wider, including allowing more banks to conduct local currency business.
The bank has applied to open a Shanghai branch in hopes of eventually gaining a licence to conduct yuan business, like nine other banks approved so far.
"We want a branch because Shanghai is a very strategic city," said a Hang Seng Bank official.
Three other Hong Kong-based banks currently have branches in Shanghai -- the Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp, the Bank of East Asia and the Po Sang Bank Ltd.
